# MCMC and model checking {#sec-mcmc-model-checking}













Let's take stock of where we actually stand. Chapter 1.1 gave us a first posterior for the ischemia effect on GFAP intensity, built on a prior that had no opinion at all. Chapter 1.2 opened up what that posterior even *is* — credibility, reallocated from prior to data via the likelihood — and used a fake dataset with a known true answer to convince ourselves the machinery works. Chapter 1.3 finally gave that model something to actually believe going in: a prior built from real reasoning about what a GFAP number can plausibly be, defended with real arguments, refit on the same fifteen animals.

That's three chapters of careful, deliberate model-building. And yet, if I'm honest with you, we still haven't asked the one question a skeptical reviewer would ask first: **does any of this actually describe the data we collected?** We've checked that the model's *machinery* runs correctly — the sampler converges, the recovery exercise in Chapter 1.2 found the truth we'd hidden in simulated data. We have not checked whether the *fitted* model, the one built on real GFAP measurements, produces predictions that look anything like those real measurements. Those are genuinely different questions, and conflating them is exactly the kind of thing that gets discovered during peer review instead of before it. This chapter closes that gap, and with it, closes Part 1 of the book.

## What is MCMC actually doing?

We've been using the term "MCMC" since Chapter 1.1, in the loosest possible way: "the machinery that draws thousands of plausible parameter values and lets them accumulate into the posterior's shape." That's true, but it's also the kind of description that lets you nod along without actually picturing anything. Let's fix that now, because understanding what's happening under the hood is the only way the diagnostics you're about to read stop being a checklist you follow on faith.

Picture the posterior as a landscape — every possible combination of parameter values (an intercept, a slope, a residual noise level) is a point on a map, and the elevation at that point is how plausible that combination is, given the priors and the data. Most of that map is nearly flat and uninteresting: wildly implausible parameter combinations, contributing almost nothing. Somewhere on it, though, there's a region of high ground — plausible combinations, clustered together — and our entire goal is to characterize the shape of that high ground: where its peak sits, how wide it is, whether it's a single smooth hill or something stranger.

The most naive way to explore that landscape is a blind random walk: stand somewhere, propose a random nearby step, and go there if it's higher ground, mostly (with some probability of accepting a step downhill too, so you don't just chase the peak and ignore its slopes). That's the classic Metropolis algorithm, and it works, in principle, on any landscape. In practice, on the many-dimensional landscapes a real model produces — even our simple two-group model has three dimensions, an intercept, a slope, and sigma, and hierarchical models later in the book will have dozens — a blind random walk spends most of its life wandering nowhere useful. It has no sense of *which direction* is uphill; it just tries steps and hopes.

Stan, the engine `brms` writes code for underneath the hood, uses something smarter: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. Think of it less like a blindfolded hiker taking random steps and more like a marble given a firm, randomly-aimed push and then left to roll, using the actual slope of the terrain to carry it efficiently across the landscape instead of stumbling across it one step at a time [@gelman2026]. Because it uses the *gradient* — literally, the slope of the plausibility surface at the marble's current position — it can propose far larger, far better-informed moves than a blind random walk ever could, which is a large part of why `brms` models with dozens of parameters remain tractable at all.

Here's the part that matters for what comes next: `brms` doesn't send out one marble, it sends out several — by default, four independent **chains**, each starting from a different random position on the landscape, each rolling its own physics-informed path and reporting back the region it explored. If the landscape is well-behaved and all four marbles genuinely explored the same high ground, we can trust that what they collectively mapped out *is* the posterior. If they didn't — if one marble got stuck on a ledge the others never visited, or the "gradient" broke down somewhere the physics simulation couldn't handle — we need to know that before we trust a single number that came out of the fit. That's exactly what the three diagnostics you've already glimpsed in Chapters 1.1 and 1.2 are built to catch. Let's take them one at a time, properly, instead of as a checklist.

::: callout-tip
### Rhat: do the marbles agree with each other?

**Rhat** compares the *between-chain* variance to the *within-chain* variance for a given parameter. If all four marbles are honestly exploring the same terrain, they should each report roughly the same spread of values for, say, the ischemia effect — and Rhat should sit right around 1. If one chain got stuck somewhere the others didn't reach, that chain's reported values will look systematically different from the rest, inflating the between-chain variance relative to the within-chain variance, and Rhat climbs above 1. **Rhat < 1.01** is the modern threshold [@gelman2026] — tighter than the "< 1.1, roughly" rule of thumb you'll find in some older references, because a value comfortably under 1.1 can still hide real disagreement between chains that a stricter, rank-based version of the statistic will catch. A high Rhat doesn't tell you *why* the chains disagree — it just tells you, honestly, that they do, and that nothing downstream of this parameter should be trusted until that's resolved.
:::

::: callout-tip
### Effective sample size: how many *independent* looks did you actually get?

Here's a subtlety worth sitting with. Each marble's next position depends on where it currently is — it doesn't teleport to a fresh, independent spot on the landscape every iteration. That means consecutive draws within a single chain are *autocorrelated*: draw number 501 looks a bit like draw number 500, which looks a bit like draw number 499. If you naively treated 4,000 MCMC draws as 4,000 independent observations of the posterior, you'd be overstating how much you actually know, in exactly the same way that counting the same animal's repeated measurements as independent replicates overstates your sample size in a pseudoreplication problem. **Effective sample size (ESS)** answers "given this autocorrelation, how many *genuinely independent-ish* draws did we effectively end up with?" — and it's reported separately for the bulk of the distribution (`ess_bulk`, governing how well you've pinned down the center) and the tails (`ess_tail`, governing how well you've pinned down the far edges, which matters directly for the width of a 95% credible interval). **Both above 400** is the standard we've used since Chapter 1.2 [@gelman2026]. A low ESS with a fine-looking Rhat is a specific, informative failure pattern: the chains agree on roughly where the high ground is, but each one is exploring it so sluggishly, taking such small, correlated steps, that you don't actually have enough *distinct* information to trust a precise summary.
:::

::: callout-important
### Divergent transitions: the sampler catching its own mistake

The first two diagnostics are both, in a sense, *summary statistics* — you compute them after the fact, from the finished chains, and they tell you about a pattern across many draws. A **divergent transition** is categorically different: it's Stan's own physics simulation flagging, in real time, that something went wrong on one specific proposed step. Recall the marble-rolling picture — Hamiltonian Monte Carlo works by numerically approximating a physical trajectory, in small discrete steps, across the landscape. In regions where the landscape's curvature changes very sharply (a steep-walled valley, a region where the plausibility surface bends abruptly), that step-by-step approximation can become numerically unstable and diverge wildly from the trajectory it's supposed to be following — the marble effectively flies off the rails. Stan detects this and flags the transition as divergent, which means the region of the posterior near that transition wasn't reliably explored, and there's no way to know from the outside how much of the posterior's true shape that unreliable region is hiding. **Zero divergent transitions** is the standard, full stop — not "a handful, but the posterior looks fine anyway." A model with divergences needs a smaller step size (`adapt_delta` closer to 1) at minimum, and often a genuine rethink of the model or its priors if divergences persist.
:::

## Revisiting the informed model from Chapter 1.3

With that mental model in hand, let's put it to work on the actual fit we care about: `informed_fit`, the model carrying the real, defended prior we built last chapter — the same formula, the same fifteen animals, cached exactly where Chapter 1.3 left it.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(here)
library(brms)
library(posterior)

cell_data <- read.csv(here("project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv"))
cell_data_sub <- subset(cell_data, DPI %in% c(0, 3))
cell_data_sub$Condition <- factor(cell_data_sub$Condition, levels = c("SHAM", "MCAO"))

priors_v1 <- c(
  prior(normal(30, 20), class = "Intercept"),
  prior(normal(0, 150), class = "b", coef = "ConditionMCAO"),
  prior(normal(0, 30), class = "sigma")
)

informed_fit <- brm(
  Gfap_Intensity ~ Condition,
  data = cell_data_sub,
  prior = priors_v1,
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/priors-regularization_fit2.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```
:::






Chapter 1.3 already reported that this fit's Rhat and ESS looked clean, in passing, before moving on to the more interesting question of what the informed prior actually changed. Let's not let that be a drive-by claim anymore — now that you know exactly what each number is checking, look at the full table:






::: {#tbl-mcmc_diagnostics .cell tbl-cap='MCMC diagnostics for the informed ischemia model, one row per parameter'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(gt)

informed_diag <- summarise_draws(as_draws_df(informed_fit), "rhat", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail")
informed_diag <- subset(informed_diag, variable %in% c("b_Intercept", "b_ConditionMCAO", "sigma"))

n_divergent <- sum(subset(nuts_params(informed_fit), Parameter == "divergent__")$Value)

stopifnot(max(informed_diag$rhat) < 1.01, min(informed_diag$ess_bulk) > 400, min(informed_diag$ess_tail) > 400)

gt(informed_diag) |> fmt_number(columns = -variable, decimals = 3)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
\begin{table}
\fontsize{12.0pt}{14.4pt}\selectfont
\begin{tabular*}{\linewidth}{@{\extracolsep{\fill}}lrrr}
\toprule
variable & rhat & ess\_bulk & ess\_tail \\ 
\midrule\addlinespace[2.5pt]
b\_Intercept & 1.002 & 2,434.932 & 1,828.582 \\ 
b\_ConditionMCAO & 1.002 & 2,554.281 & 2,443.052 \\ 
sigma & 1.001 & 2,357.940 & 2,201.685 \\ 
\bottomrule
\end{tabular*}
\end{table}

:::
:::






Every Rhat in that table sits at 1.002, both effective sample sizes clear 400 for all three parameters, and we count 0 divergent transitions across every chain. Given what you now know each of those numbers is actually checking — chain agreement, effective independence, the sampler's own error flag — that's a fit we can trust to have explored its posterior honestly.

Numbers in a table are one kind of evidence; a rank overlay plot is a more direct visual version of the same Rhat check, and it's worth seeing at least once so a table full of 1.00s isn't the only form this diagnostic ever takes for you. If the four chains are genuinely exploring the same landscape, each chain's draws, ranked and pooled together, should look uniformly scattered across the full range of ranks — no chain should be systematically stuck reporting only low or only high values relative to the others.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mcmc_plot(informed_fit, type = "rank_overlay", pars = c("b_Intercept", "b_ConditionMCAO", "sigma")) +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Rank overlay plot for the informed model's three parameters — each colored line is one chain's ranked draws, and they should overlap like this](mcmc-model-checking_files/figure-pdf/fig-mcmc_rank_overlay-1.pdf){#fig-mcmc_rank_overlay}
:::
:::






Four roughly flat, overlapping lines, no chain systematically riding above or below the others — exactly the picture Rhat's single number was already telling us, just made visible instead of abstracted into a statistic.

::: callout-tip
### Frequentist equivalent

There isn't really a parallel step here — this whole diagnostic layer is specific to the Bayesian fit, a consequence of estimating the posterior by simulation rather than by a closed-form formula. `lm()` doesn't sample anything, so it has nothing analogous to converge or fail to converge; its "did the numbers come out right" question is answered by different machinery entirely (numerical stability of the underlying matrix algebra, which is rarely an issue for a model this simple). This is one of the real costs of the Bayesian approach, worth naming honestly rather than glossing over: you get a full posterior distribution and the flexibility to fold in real prior knowledge, but you also inherit a whole extra layer of "did my estimation procedure actually work" that a frequentist fit doesn't ask you to check.
:::

## Does the model actually describe our data? The posterior predictive check

Here's the thing about everything we've just verified: it tells us the sampler explored the posterior honestly. It says nothing at all about whether that posterior — however faithfully explored — actually describes the biology in front of us. A perfectly converged model can still be a bad model. MCMC diagnostics are quality control on the *exploration*; what we need now is quality control on the *destination*.

Think about how you'd actually settle this with a skeptical colleague. You wouldn't show them Rhat. You'd say: "here's what my fitted model thinks GFAP data should look like — now here's what I actually measured. You tell me if you can spot the difference." That comparison, done properly and repeatedly rather than as a single eyeballed glance, is exactly what a **posterior predictive check (PPC)** is. Formally: draw a large number of parameter sets from the posterior, and for each one, simulate a brand-new dataset the same size and shape as the real one, using the model's own likelihood — the same generative move we practiced in Chapter 1.2, except now the parameters feeding it come from a posterior fit to real data instead of numbers we picked ourselves. If the fitted model is a reasonable description of reality, those simulated datasets, taken as a group, should be hard to tell apart from the real one. As McElreath puts it, a Bayesian model is generative by construction — it can always simulate new observations from its own parameters — and a posterior predictive check is simply that generative machinery, pointed at its own fit, as a form of self-criticism [@mcelreath2020].

::: callout-note
### A deliberate shortcut, for now

A honest posterior predictive check is, at its core, "compare two distributions visually" — which is precisely what the exploratory data analysis part of this book, coming right after this chapter, is going to teach you to do properly with `ggplot2`: density plots, overlaid distributions, the whole toolkit. We haven't gotten there yet, and I'd rather not ask you to half-learn distributional plotting on the fly, buried inside a chapter about something else. So for this chapter, we lean entirely on `brms`'s and `bayesplot`'s turnkey `pp_check()` function — it does exactly the comparison we need, out of the box, no custom plotting required. Once Part 2 has given you real `ggplot2` fluency with distributions, nothing stops a later chapter from coming back to this exact output and rebuilding it by hand, with more control over the presentation. That's a job for that future chapter, not this one.
:::






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pp_check(informed_fit, ndraws = 100) +
  labs(x = "GFAP intensity", y = "Density") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Posterior predictive check — simulated GFAP datasets from the fitted informed model (thin lines) against the real observed data (dark line)](mcmc-model-checking_files/figure-pdf/fig-mcmc_ppc_dens-1.pdf){#fig-mcmc_ppc_dens}
:::
:::






The dark line is the density of our fifteen real GFAP measurements. Every thin line is a full dataset the fitted model simulated from one posterior draw. What we're looking for is exactly what a spot-the-difference puzzle asks of you: does the dark line sit comfortably inside that cloud of simulated curves, or does it stick out somewhere the model never predicted? Here, it sits right in the thick of the cloud — the model isn't systematically missing the shape of what we actually measured.

But "eyeball the overall shape" is a coarse check, and Chapter 1.3 left us with a specific, concrete worry we shouldn't let slide just because the overall density looks fine: our Gaussian model has no built-in knowledge that GFAP intensity can't be negative, and the *prior*-only simulation back in that chapter put real mass below zero. Has fitting the model to real data fixed that, or is it still lurking in the posterior predictions we'd actually report? Let's check it directly instead of assuming the dense-looking overlap above already answered it — we'll reload that same prior-only fit from Chapter 1.3 (cached, no refitting) and compare its simulated negative values against the informed posterior's:






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
prior_check_fit <- brm(
  Gfap_Intensity ~ Condition,
  data = cell_data_sub,
  prior = priors_v1,
  sample_prior = "only",
  seed = 123,
  file = "models/priors-regularization_fit1.rds",
  file_refit = "never"
)
```
:::








Before any real data had spoken, about 35.5% of the values our priors alone were willing to propose were negative — a genuinely sizeable blind spot, which makes sense: a prior alone has nothing but our stated ranges to go on, and those ranges were deliberately generous. After fitting to the real fifteen animals, that fraction drops to 6.4%. The data pulled the model's predictions decisively toward the plausible range, the same way it pulled the ischemia-effect estimate in Chapter 1.3 — but a Gaussian likelihood still has no hard floor at zero, so the blind spot doesn't vanish entirely, it just shrinks by roughly a factor of five. We can see exactly where that shows up by checking the model's simulated *minimum* value against the real one, rather than just the shape of the whole curve:






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
pp_check(informed_fit, type = "stat", stat = "min", ndraws = 2000) +
  labs(x = "Minimum simulated GFAP intensity", y = "Count") +
  Plot_theme
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Posterior predictive check on the minimum simulated value — the observed minimum (dark line) against the distribution of minimums from 2,000 simulated datasets](mcmc-model-checking_files/figure-pdf/fig-mcmc_ppc_min-1.pdf){#fig-mcmc_ppc_min}
:::
:::






The real minimum sits inside the bulk of the simulated distribution rather than off in an extreme tail, so on the data we actually have — sham animals with a comfortable baseline, well clear of zero — this isn't a check that's currently failing us. But it's a check we should keep running on faith as-is, not one we've *solved*: shrink that sham baseline, or push into a dataset with genuinely low-intensity animals, and this exact same Gaussian assumption would start producing predictions no biologist would accept. Flagging that honestly here, rather than pretending a shrinking-but-nonzero fraction is the same as zero, is precisely the point of running this check at all.

::: callout-tip
### Frequentist equivalent

The structurally equivalent step on the frequentist side is residual diagnostics: does the pattern of leftover variation, once the model's fitted values are subtracted out, look the way the model assumes it should? For our `lm()` fit, that means a residuals-vs-fitted plot (checking for patterns the model's structure should have captured but didn't) and a Q-Q plot (checking the normality assumption the model's inference leans on).






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(parsnip)
library(broom)

parsnip_model <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(Gfap_Intensity ~ Condition, data = cell_data_sub)

lm_diag <- augment(parsnip_model$fit)

p1 <- ggplot(lm_diag, aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Fitted value", y = "Residual") +
  Plot_theme

p2 <- ggplot(lm_diag, aes(sample = .resid)) +
  stat_qq(color = "#0072B2", size = 2) +
  stat_qq_line(color = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantiles", y = "Sample quantiles") +
  Plot_theme

library(patchwork)
p1 + p2
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![Frequentist residual diagnostics for the same ischemia model](mcmc-model-checking_files/figure-pdf/fig-mcmc_lm_diagnostics-1.pdf){#fig-mcmc_lm_diagnostics}
:::
:::






Both diagnostics are asking essentially the same underlying question a posterior predictive check asks — does the fitted model's account of the noise match the noise we actually observe — just from the frequentist side of the fence, using a single fitted line and its leftovers rather than an entire posterior of simulated datasets. What the Bayesian PPC buys you that a residual plot alone can't: a *distribution* over how extreme a statistic like "the minimum simulated value" could plausibly be, rather than one fixed set of residuals to eyeball. That difference matters more the smaller and noisier your data gets — which is exactly the situation Chapter 1.3 showed you a prior can help with, and this chapter has now shown you how to actually check.
:::

## When a check fails: closing the loop

We got lucky, in a sense — every check in this chapter came back clean enough to trust. It's worth being explicit about what happens when one doesn't, because it will, eventually, on some model in your own work, and I don't want the only example you've seen to be one where everything just worked.

Go back to the model-infer-check-improve loop from Chapter 1.2. A failed posterior predictive check isn't a dead end, and it isn't a verdict that Bayesian modeling "doesn't work" — it's the **check** step doing exactly its job, catching a mismatch between what your model assumes and what your data actually looks like, so that you can act on it before anyone downstream trusts a number that doesn't deserve it. The specific fix depends entirely on what the check revealed: a systematically bad group-wise tail might call for a different response family (we'll meet several once Part 3 gets to GLMs — Poisson and negative binomial for counts, beta regression for proportions, all built for outcomes a plain Gaussian can't honestly represent); a mismatch concentrated in one particular subgroup might point to a missing predictor rather than the wrong family entirely. We're not solving that here — our checks didn't demand it — but naming the next move now means you'll recognize it as a normal, expected part of the workflow the first time a check of your own comes back genuinely unhappy, rather than something to be embarrassed about.

## Closing Part 1

Look back at the arc these four chapters actually walked. We started with a single worked example and a model that didn't know anything going in — a deliberately naive first pass, so we'd have something honest to improve on. We opened up what a posterior really represents, and used a positive control with a known answer to earn our trust in the fitting machinery itself. We replaced that model's flat default with a prior built from real reasoning, and watched it do real work exactly where a frequentist fit has no equivalent lever to pull — a small, noisy sample. And in this chapter, we finally asked the question we'd been quietly deferring since Chapter 1.1: not just "did the sampler behave," but "does the fitted model actually look like the data we collected" — and we now know precisely what each of the standard MCMC diagnostics is protecting us from, not just that we're supposed to check them.

That's the whole apparatus of Bayesian inference, built once, on one small dataset, so that every applied chapter from here forward can lean on it without re-deriving it. What we still haven't done, on purpose, is *really* look at `cell_data` — no formal distributions, no relationships between variables, no hunting for the kind of structure that would make you rethink a model before you've even fit it. That's exactly where we're headed next. Part 2 opens the dataset back up and teaches you to see it properly, with the `ggplot2` fluency this chapter deliberately borrowed against by leaning on `pp_check()` instead — and everything you learn there will, eventually, loop right back around to sharpening the very posterior predictive checks this chapter just introduced.
